pages.text: 3/8 and 5/8 of the same bar are both counted in eighths, so the pieces are the same size. When the bottoms match, the bigger top is the bigger fraction.

pages.name: Colour more than 2/5
pages.task: Colour more than 2/5 of the bottom bar.
pages.why: Both bars are cut into fifths, so more fifths make a bigger fraction. 3/5, 4/5 and 5/5 are all bigger than 2/5.

pages.name: Sixths or thirds
pages.why: A sixth is half of a third, so 2/6 is half of 2/3. The bigger bottom names the smaller piece.

pages.name: Eighths or quarters
pages.why: Give both eighths. 2/4 = 4/8, and 4 eighths are more than 3.

pages.name: Thirds or quarters
pages.task: Which is bigger, 2/3 or 3/4? The fine lines cut both bars into twelfths, since 3 × 4 = 12.
pages.why: Each third is cut into 4 twelfths and each quarter into 3. So 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, and 9 is more than 8.

pages.task: Divide the top by the bottom. What is 5/8 as a decimal?
pages.why: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625. It sits at the same place on the line as 5/8.

pages.name: Two drill bits
pages.task: Which drill bit is bigger, 7/16 inch or 1/2 inch?
pages.why: A half is 8 sixteenths, so 1/2 inch = 8/16 inch. That is 1/16 inch more than 7/16 inch.

pages.name: Three in order
pages.task: Tap these in order, smallest first.
pages.why: As decimals, 5/8 = 0.625, 2/3 = 0.666… and 3/4 = 0.75. So 5/8 is the smallest and 3/4 the biggest.

pages.alt: Two bars of the same length, labelled 10/16 and 5/8, cut into sixteenths and eighths, and shaded. Each eighth is cut into 2, so 5/8 = 10/16. A line at the end of the shading shows both end at the same place.
